d.title: How SharePot Perp works
d.intro: SharePot Perp is a set of pools, one per stock: {list}, as Coinbase's tokenized stocks on Base ({toks}). In each pool you put that stock's token in and pick what it should do: twice the stock's daily move, its dollar value locked, or a bet on it falling. Once a day, at the official close, the side that lost moves tokens to the side that won. Nobody borrows, so nobody is ever liquidated. The examples below use {sym}; every pool works the same way, each on its own stock.
d.why.h: Why put a stock token in here
d.why.b:
• Twice the move, no margin account. Like a 2x ETF on {sym} (NVDL), but with the token you already hold, no broker, and no liquidation price.
  • Lock its value without selling. Before earnings, say: the hedge tier keeps your position's dollar value where it is, and the other side pays you funding while longs are the crowd.
  • Short it with the token itself. Again without borrowing anything.
  • Tokens in, tokens out. You put in {tok} and take out {tok}. Nothing is sold and there is no stablecoin anywhere in the pool.
d.tiers.b:

Why no Long 1x? That is just holding {tok} in your wallet: no pool needed.

Why at most 2x long? {sym}'s worst day since 1999 was −35.2% (6 Aug 2004). A 3x long would have gone to zero that day; a 2x long kept 30%. Its best day, +42.4%, would have left Short 2x with 15%. TSLA's worst day since 2010 was −21.1% (8 Sep 2020) and META's since 2012 −26.4% (3 Feb 2022). A stock is listed only if its worst day stays above −50%, so Long 2x has never been wiped out on any of them; that is why Apple is not here (−51.9% on 29 Sep 2000).

If you know coin-margined perps: Long 2x is a 1x long with the coin as margin, Hedge is a 1x short, Short 1x a 2x short, Short 2x a 3x short — settled once a day, never liquidated.
d.day.b:
1. Before the closing bell (16:00 in New York, shown in your own time on every page) you request an entry or an exit. Requests after the bell go to the next trading day.
  2. About 30 minutes after the bell the close is proposed on-chain once the sources agree: Yahoo's close must match Nasdaq's official close to the cent (if Nasdaq has not published it within two hours, Yahoo is used alone and the evidence says so), and Chainlink's {sym} price on Base mainnet must be within 1%.
  3. For 6 hours the proposal can be disputed. A second server recomputes it from the same public sources and, if it differs, rejects it with a key that can do nothing else; the operator then proposes again. The operator can never propose a move of more than 50% in a day.
  4. Then the day settles, all at that close: the price move, the funding, the exits, the entries.
  5. Your entry is your position from then on, with no claim to make. Your exit waits in the contract until you press Withdraw.
d.money.b:
• Only the matched part moves. Long exposure is the tokens in the long tier times its in-pool multiple; short exposure is the same on the short side. The smaller side is matched in full, the bigger side pro rata — that share is its fill. The unmatched part of a deposit simply holds the stock, so your real leverage depends on the pool. It is always shown before you enter.
  • Price. At each close the losing side pays the winning side its in-pool multiple × fill × the move, in tokens, capped at what the tier holds.
  • Funding. Each day: 0.1% × (long − short) ÷ (long + short), paid by the crowded side to the thin side, on the matched part only. Never more than 0.1% a day.
  • Fees. 0.1% on the way in and 0.1% on the way out, taken in the pool's own token. An entry taken back before its bell pays the entry fee too. They become the platform's own hedge position, so the platform always sits on the value-locked side.
  • Everything compounds. Gains, losses and funding stay in your position. Leverage resets daily like a 2x ETF: up 10% then down 10% leaves the stock at −1% but 2x at −4%.
  • No liquidations, no debt. One close beyond a tier's zero line takes that tier to zero — never below, nobody owes anything, and intraday prices never count.
  • Dividends. The pool settles on total return: a dividend going ex that day is added back to the close, so the mechanical ex-dividend drop is no gift to the shorts.
d.check.b: Every close goes on-chain together with the sha256 of a file that holds the price sources' raw answers. The Daily closes page shows, for each day, the close, Nasdaq's second opinion, the Chainlink comparison, what moved between the sides and the funding, with the transactions — and a Check button that downloads the evidence file and hashes it in your browser, so you can see it matches the hash stored on-chain.
d.trust.b:
• The operator key schedules the trading days (never more than 30 days ahead) and proposes each close. It cannot propose a move over 50% in a day, and every proposal waits 6 hours before it can settle. It can skip a day with no usable close (its requests roll to the next day), but only before the next day's close, so it can never choose with the next close already known.
  • The checker's key, on a second server, can only reject a proposal: it cannot propose, settle, skip or change anything.
  • The admin key can reject a proposal, pause new requests, move the cutoff of a day that has not closed yet, and change the fee and funding rates within hard caps (1% fee, 1% a day funding). It can also propose a close itself, with no 50% cap, and settle it at once: the way out for a real day beyond 50%. In the wrong hands that key could move value between the sides, so on mainnet it would sit behind a multisig. It cannot take tokens out of the pool.
  • Nothing waits on us. After the dispute window anyone can settle a day, and anyone can withdraw an exit — the tokens always go to their owner.
  • The token's issuer (Coinbase, for the real {toks}) can pause transfers or block addresses, this pool included. This testnet uses stand-in tokens ({toks}) that anyone can mint, up to 10,000 per transaction.
  • The US block lives on this website, not in the contract: the contract cannot see where a wallet is. Visitors Cloudflare places in the United States can read every page, but every button that sends a transaction is off.
  • Approval. Your first entry in a pool asks your wallet to let that pool take its token. The pool only takes it when you request an entry; there is no amount limit, like most apps, and you can revoke it in your wallet at any time.
  • Not available to persons in the United States.
d.try.b:
1. Connect a wallet, or pick the test wallet that lives in your browser.
  2. On the Faucet page, press Get 100 test … for any of {toks}. A fresh wallet first gets a little test ETH for fees.
  3. Pick a tier, type an amount, and read the preview: the multiple when fully matched, your fill today, your real leverage, the funding, the zero line.
  4. Enter. You are in at the next close.
  5. Come back after it settles: your position is on the pool page and in My activity.
d.contracts.old: Older pools: no new entries, still settled every trading day so whoever is in them can exit and withdraw.
d.contracts.api: Read-only JSON, no key: /api/days?s=<SYMBOL> every day with its close, evidence summary and transactions · /api/evidence/<SYMBOL>/<day> the evidence file, byte for byte · /api/activity/<address> one wallet's requests and withdrawals · /api/health.
d.faq.b:
What if nobody is on the other side?
Then your deposit just holds {sym} (1x long) and pays no funding. Your leverage starts as the other side fills up.
Can I lose more than I put in?
No. A tier can go to zero, never below.
Can I take back an entry?
Yes, until the bell: press Cancel next to it on the pool page and it comes back at once, less the 0.1% entry fee. After the bell the close is known, so an entry can no longer be taken back: it is filled, and you exit at a later close.
When do I get my tokens back?
Request an exit before a bell. It fills at that close, settles about 6.5 hours later, and then you press Withdraw.
Why single stocks and not an index?
Coinbase's tokenized stocks on Base are all single stocks: 358 of them in mid-November 2026, no ETFs.
Can I be in more than one pool?
Yes. Each stock is its own pool, with its own token, closes, funding and contract; a position in one never touches another. My activity shows them all.
Why a testnet?
This is a build for Base Stocks Maxxing Season. The mechanism is the same on mainnet with the real {toks}.
d.ours.b: On this testnet a few wallets that trade in the pool are ours, so that both sides have money in. They are never presented as users.
d.ours.treasury: platform treasury: fees and the platform's hedge
